analysis.one_liner: Designates the Arctic Refuge coastal plain as wilderness, permanently banning oil drilling there.
analysis.headline: The bill to protect 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic Refuge never got a committee vote or a Senate floor action, dying after two years in committee with 33 Senate supporters.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make about 1.56 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain part of the National Wilderness Preservation System. Wilderness status is the strongest land protection federal law offers: it bars roads, motorized vehicles, and any development, which would permanently end the push to drill for oil in the refuge. The bill was introduced in February 2021 with 32 cosponsors, all Democrats and independents, and was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up before Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public gets permanent protection of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain — the calving ground of the Porcupine caribou herd and habitat the Gwich'in people have relied on for subsistence for generations — with no cost to taxpayers. Future generations keep the area undeveloped, and the public is spared the air, water, and climate effects of new drilling in a fragile ecosystem.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and Alaska Native subsistence communities

how_it_helps.text: The bill designates approximately 1,559,538 acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge in Alaska as a component of the National Wilderness Preservation System.

Wilderness designation under the Wilderness Act prohibits roads, motorized access, and development, which would permanently prevent oil and gas drilling in the coastal plain — the area Congress in 2017 opened to a mandated lease sale program.
The protected area is the calving ground of the Porcupine caribou herd, and permanent protection preserves the subsistence way of life for communities that depend on the herd.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose access to what the government has estimated holds significant recoverable oil. The federal Treasury and the state of Alaska forgo lease-bid payments and future royalties that drilling would have produced. A handful of Alaska Native communities on the coastal plain that supported drilling as a source of jobs and revenue lose that economic option.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil drillers, Alaska's treasury, pro-drilling villages

drawbacks.text: Permanent wilderness status closes off an estimated multi-billion-barrel oil resource on federal land, forgoing lease-bid revenue and royalties that would have flowed to the federal Treasury and to the state of Alaska, which shares in federal oil revenue.

Some Alaska Native communities on the coastal plain, such as Kaktovik, supported drilling because the area holds few other economic opportunities; the bill forecloses that option with no substitute provided.

The designation is irreversible in practice — Congress almost never undoes wilderness — so opponents argue future generations would be locked out of the resource no matter what energy conditions look like.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a permanent, irrevocable protection of a rare, intact Arctic ecosystem against forgoing oil revenue and drilling jobs in a single remote area. For most Americans the protection is the larger value; the honest cost is real but concentrated — lease revenue to the Treasury, Alaska's share of royalties, and a few villages' hopes for local development. The main design criticism is that it settles the question permanently rather than by scientific or economic review.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee in February 2021, the committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Arctic Refuge Protection Act of 2021 on February 8, 2021, joined by 28 other Democratic senators as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
The bill finished with 32 cosponsors, all 32 Democrats or independents, and no Republican support.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no vote, no floor consideration — and the bill expired with the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas interests kept the Arctic Refuge coastal plain open to potential drilling, since wilderness protection never became law; the 2017 mandate for coastal plain lease sales stayed on the books. Everyone who valued permanent protection of the refuge lost the opportunity.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas interests kept drilling open

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 28 original cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 Senate supporters were Democrats or independents — 31 of 48 Democrats plus 1 of 2 independents — and no Republican signed on, so the bill faced no realistic path to the 60-vote level wilderness bills typically need; the Democratic-led committee also declined to advance it.

industries.industry: Oil and gas exploration and drilling
industries.note: The bill would have permanently locked the drillers out of the Arctic Refuge coastal plain, which Congress had already opened to a mandated lease sale in 2017. Industry gains from drilling (lease purchases, production) come at the cost of developing an intact public wilderness the public would otherwise retain.

industries.industry: Alaska state government and local economies near the refuge
industries.note: The state and a few nearby villages would forgo lease revenue, shared royalties, and jobs that drilling would have brought. Some Alaska Native communities favored drilling for this reason, while Gwich'in communities downstream of the calving grounds opposed it to protect the caribou they subsist on.
